event: Elsie wakes in Tamsin's narrow bunk with Tamsin's arm heavy across her waist.
prose: Elsie woke to the slap of water against the hull and a dark square of window above her head, and for a moment did not know where she was. Then she smelled coal and canal and soap, and felt the narrow mattress under her hip, and the wall at her back, and something heavy and warm lying across her waist. It was Tamsin's arm. It lay over her in the quilt, slack and heavy, the hand open against Elsie's stomach through her shift, the freckled wrist turned up. Elsie looked down at it and smiled, and did not move, so as not to wake her.

event: Tamsin is awake and very still, and says good morning to the ceiling.
prose: But Tamsin was awake. Elsie could tell from her breathing, which was very quiet and very careful, and from how still she lay, stiller than any sleeper, her whole long body gone rigid along Elsie's side. Elsie turned her head on the pillow. Tamsin was lying on her back with her eyes open, looking straight up at the planks of the cabin roof, and her face was red to the hairline. Her arm did not move from Elsie's waist. "Morning," Tamsin said to the ceiling. Her voice came out hoarse. "Good morning. Did you. Sleep. All right." "Lovely," Elsie said, and yawned, and snuggled down.

event: Rosa is already frying bread on the black stove and singing, and Nell is up on deck.
prose: The cabin was full of the smell of frying. Rosa stood at the black stove in her faded red shirt with her sleeves pushed up, turning slices of bread in a pan of sizzling fat with her fingers, and singing under her breath, a slow wharf song with a lot of verses about a drowned bargeman. The lamp was out and the grey light came in through the geraniums. Nell's shelf of a bunk over the stove was empty, the blanket thrown back, and through the open hatch Elsie heard her up on deck, whistling and coiling rope and talking to a gull as if it owed her money.

event: Over breakfast Elsie remembers the flower cart notice, and says she must go to the guild.
prose: They ate fried bread at the folding table with mugs of strong tea, the four of them crammed elbow to elbow again, and Rosa put an egg on everyone's plate whether they wanted one or not. Elsie was halfway through hers when she remembered. She put down her fork. "Oh," she said. "The flower cart." They all looked at her. "There's a notice on the board," Elsie said. "At the guild. An escort, for a flower cart round the lake villages. I saw it two days ago and I meant to ask Tilly, and then—" She looked at Tamsin. "I ought to go to the guild."

event: Nell makes Tamsin promise to come back for supper tonight, before the Marigold goes.
prose: Nell looked up sharply from her egg. "You're going," she said to Tamsin, not to Elsie. "Off to the city with her, the minute you've eaten." Tamsin opened her mouth. "Then you come back," Nell said. "Tonight. For supper. We're loading all day and we go through the lock in the morning, and you're not to just walk off up that lane and leave it another year. You promise me." She put down her fork and pointed it across the table at her sister, and her chin had gone stubborn and square. "Say it. Say you'll come back for supper."

memory.fact: Tamsin promised Nell and Rosa to come back to the Marigold for supper on the seventh.

event: Tamsin promises, and Nell makes her say it to Rosa too.
prose: "I promise," Tamsin said. She said it to her plate, low, and then lifted her head and said it again to Nell's face. "I promise. I'll come back for supper." Nell narrowed her green eyes at her. "Say it to Mum," she said. "Nell—" "Say it to Mum. She'll hold you to it. I'm only your sister." Tamsin turned on the bench to Rosa at the stove, and Rosa turned round with the pan in her hand, and waited. "I'll come back for supper, Mum," Tamsin said. Rosa nodded once, slowly, and turned back to the stove, and Elsie saw her wipe her eyes on her shoulder.

event: Rosa hugs Elsie at the plank and asks for a slice of the next cake.
prose: Rosa came out to the plank to see them off, in her apron with her shawl round her shoulders against the early chill. She hugged Tamsin first, for a long time, without saying anything. Then she turned and hugged Elsie, a big coal-smelling hug that lifted Elsie onto her toes and squeezed the breath out of her. "You," Rosa said into her hair. "You come back too. Any time we're in." She set Elsie down and held her off by the shoulders and looked at her. "And next time you bake that cake," she said, "you save me a slice. A big one. I'll know if it's small."

event: Elsie and Tamsin walk back through the city in the mist off the Mere.
prose: The city was white with mist. It came up off the Mere in the early mornings and lay along the canals, thick and soft and cool, so that the water vanished under it and the bridges rose out of it into white and the far banks were only shapes. The paper lanterns hung along the towpaths unlit and beaded with wet. Elsie and Tamsin walked back the way they had come, over bridge after bridge, their footsteps loud on the stones. A baker's boy went by with a tray on his head. A cat sat on a bollard, damp and offended. Elsie breathed the cool air and felt full of the barge still.

pictured.coverAfter: The city was white with mist. It came up off the Mere
pictured.outfit: cropped cream halter top laced up the front, short sage-green skirt, brown belt with pouches, fingerless gloves, tall boots and healer's satchel

event: Tamsin is quiet, and twice bumps Elsie's shoulder on purpose.
prose: Tamsin was quiet. She walked beside Elsie with her hands in her pockets and her hair springing loose from its comb in the damp, and she did not say much, but it was a different quiet from yesterday's: Elsie could feel it down the Tether, and it was not cold or held. It was something more like the slow warm feel of a full stomach. On the second bridge Tamsin bumped Elsie's shoulder with hers, on purpose, and then looked away over the canal as if she had not. On the fourth she did it again. Elsie bumped her back, and Tamsin's mouth twitched at one corner.

pictured.coverAfter: Tamsin was quiet. She walked beside Elsie with her hands in her
pictured.outfit: faded green shirt with the sleeves rolled, dark trousers, knuckle wraps and scuffed boots

event: Elsie says Nell is wonderful; Tamsin says yes, and that she will answer every letter.
prose: "Nell is wonderful," Elsie said, as they came down off the fifth bridge. "She's so quick. And funny. And she's got your grin, did you know? Exactly. And she loves you so much, Tamsin." Tamsin was quiet for a few steps. "Yes," she said at last. "She is." She took one hand out of her pocket and rubbed the back of her neck. "I took the letters," she said. "The bundle. They're inside my shirt." She patted the place, over her heart. "I'm going to answer every one. All of them. Even the one about the heron. I'll be at it a month." She grinned, crooked. "She'll have to post me the next lot."

event: The guild hall is just opening, and a sunburnt carter waits by the F-rank board.
prose: The guild hall was only just opening. A clerk was propping the great doors back with wedges, and inside the lamps were still being lit along the beams, and the long hall smelled of floor polish and cold ashes. There were few adventurers yet: two at the tea counter, yawning, and one asleep on a bench with his hat over his face. By the F-rank end of the quest board a woman stood waiting with her arms folded. She was small and broad and sunburnt to the colour of a brick, in a straw hat and a smock with dried petals stuck to it, and she was frowning at the board.

event: She says her escort notice has gone untaken two days, and the reed sprites rob her blind.
prose: She turned as they came up, and looked them over, Tamsin's axe and Elsie's satchel, and her frown eased a little. "You after a job?" she said. "Because I've a job. That one." She jabbed a thick finger at a notice on the board: the flower cart, round the lake villages, five lanterns. "Two days it's hung there, untaken. Too far, too dull, not enough pay, they say." She spat to one side, neatly. "And meanwhile the reed sprites rob me blind. Every trip. My roses, my ribbons, my good red hat. I'm not asking for heroes. I'm asking for somebody to swat."

memory.fact: From the fifth the F-rank board has: escort a flower cart round the lake villages, five lanterns.

event: Tilly runs in with her braids half done, and stops dead to see them come in together.
prose: The doors banged. Tilly came in at a run, with her goggles bouncing on her head and her apron flapping and her belt of vials clinking, and one braid done and the other half done and coming loose, its tie in her teeth. She came skidding up the hall toward the board, saw Elsie, beamed round the tie, and then saw Tamsin beside her, close beside her, at this hour of the morning, the two of them come in together through the same door, and stopped dead in the middle of the floor. She took the tie out of her mouth. Her bright blue eyes went from one of them to the other.

pictured.coverAfter: The doors banged. Tilly came in at a run, with her goggles
pictured.outfit: cream blouse with rolled sleeves, too-big scorched apron and belt of corked vials

event: She asks where Elsie was last night; she knocked at the Honeycomb with a pear fizz.
prose: "Elsie," Tilly said. "Where were you? Last night?" She came the rest of the way slowly, holding the tie. "I came round. To the Honeycomb. I knocked. I brought a pear fizz, a fresh one, the new kind, I put the pear in later this time like I said, and I thought we could have it on your window sill and look at the canal." She pushed her loose hair back. "And you weren't there. I knocked twice. The baker came down and said you'd gone out with a cake in the morning and not come back, and looked at me, and I didn't know where you were."

event: Elsie says she slept on Tamsin's mother's barge, in Tamsin's bunk, and Tilly goes very quiet.
prose: "Oh, Tilly, I'm so sorry," Elsie said, and meant it. "I'd have loved a fizz. I was on Tamsin's mother's barge, on the Long Cut. We took the cake, and her mum and her sister made us stay for supper, and then it was late and her mum said to sleep aboard, so I did." She smiled at the memory. "In Tamsin's bunk. It's tiny. We had to share." Tilly went very quiet. She stood with the tie in her fingers and looked at Elsie, and then at Tamsin, and then at the floor between her own boots, and her face did something small and careful, and she said, "Oh."

memory.fact: Elsie and Tamsin slept the night of the sixth together in Tamsin's bunk on the Marigold.
Elsie and Tamsin slept the night of the sixth together in Tamsin's bunk on the Marigold.

event: Elsie finishes Tilly's braid for her unasked, and Tilly stands like a statue.
prose: Elsie saw the half-done braid coming loose over Tilly's shoulder. She took the tie gently out of Tilly's fingers, without asking, and stepped round behind her, and undid the loose part and combed it through with her fingers, the long fair hair with its singed ends, and began to plait it again from the nape of her neck. Tilly went perfectly still. She stood in the middle of the guild hall like a statue, with her arms at her sides and her eyes fixed straight ahead on the quest board, and did not move at all while Elsie plaited, except that her ears went slowly pink.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 21 → 22 (kindness: Elsie finishes her braid)

event: Cora comes out of the charcoal door, and Elsie asks if she slept well.
prose: Elsie tied off the braid and patted it. The charcoal-painted door across the hall opened, and Cora came out, buttoned to the throat, with the ledger under her arm and her black hair drawn back so tight and smooth it shone under the lamps. She came straight across to them and took her place, a step behind Elsie, and inclined her head. "Fairweather." "Good morning, Cora," Elsie said, turning round to her with a smile. "Did you sleep well?" Cora looked at her. There was a small pause. "Adequately," she said. Then, after another moment: "Thank you." She opened the ledger.

event: The clerk enters the party for the flower cart, and Cora writes it in her ledger.
prose: The carter took them to the clerk's desk, where a thin young clerk with ink on his fingers wrote out the escort in a big book: the flower cart, the lake villages, this party, and their names, one under another. Elsie signed her own in round careful letters, and Tamsin scrawled hers, and Tilly wrote hers very small. The clerk blotted it and stamped it. Beside them Cora wrote in her ledger at the same time, in her small exact hand, the date and the notice and the names, and Elsie, watching her pen, saw her own name come out at the top of the line.

event: Long past the cart's usual dawn start, they set out from the flower market with it.
prose: The flower cart stood waiting at the old flower market, a donkey cart with high slatted sides, stacked with empty buckets, and a grey donkey between the shafts with a straw hat of its own on, holes cut for its ears. "Should've been gone at dawn," the carter said, climbing up onto the seat. "We go at dawn. Back by dusk. That's the round. We'll be tight for it today, and that's on account of waiting for you lot, so I'll thank you not to dawdle." She clicked her tongue. The donkey sighed and leaned into the collar, and the cart rolled out over the cobbles, and they walked beside it.

event: The shore road runs between lavender and poppy fields and the reed beds of the Mere.
prose: Past the last houses the city fell away, and the shore road ran out along the Mere in the sun. The mist had burned off. On the right hand the lavender fields rolled away up the slope in long purple rows, humming with bees, and between them stood fields of poppies so red they hurt to look at; on the left hand were the reed beds, tall and green and whispering, and beyond them the flat bright water of the Mere going all the way to the sky. The road was white dust between the two, and the cart's wheels squeaked, and the air smelled of lavender and warm water.

event: Elsie walks with her hand trailing through the lavender, humming.
prose: Elsie walked on the lavender side. She let her hand trail out beside her through the tops of the nearest row as she went, so that the flower heads brushed her palm and bobbed back behind her, and her fingers came away smelling sweet and sharp, and she held them to her nose and then let them trail again. A bee came with her hand for a while, and went. The sun was warm on her bare shoulders. Without noticing, she began to hum, the caravan song from yesterday, and the cart squeaked along in time, and Tamsin, on the reed side, looked across at her and smiled.

memory.fact: Now and then Elsie hums without knowing it.

event: The carter says there are four villages: Sweetwater, Larkford, Pennyfield and Reedby.
prose: "Four villages on the round," the carter said from the seat, without being asked, flicking the reins at a fly on the donkey's rump. "Sweetwater first, that's roses. Then Larkford, that's poppies. Then Pennyfield, where there's the Poppy inn and we stop to eat, and then Reedby at the far end, which is all sorts. Lavender, cornflowers, sweet peas. Few miles apart, each of them." She spat again, neatly. "Sweetwater, Larkford, Pennyfield, Reedby. And back. You'll know them in your sleep by the end." Elsie said them over to herself, softly, so as to keep them: Sweetwater, Larkford, Pennyfield, Reedby.

event: At Sweetwater the growers load buckets of roses, and Elsie helps carry them.
prose: Sweetwater was a cluster of white cottages round a green with a pump, and every garden was roses: climbing the walls, spilling over the gates, standing in rows in the fields behind in every colour from cream to near-black. The growers had the buckets waiting at the roadside, rows of them, packed with long-stemmed blooms in water. Elsie took one in both arms. It was heavier than it looked, the water slopping cold against her chest, and she staggered with it to the cart and lifted it up to the carter, and went back for another, and another, with petals sticking to her arms and her halter damp.

event: Tilly sniffs every rose and names the oils in it, fast, and the growers stare.
prose: Tilly had stopped at the first bucket and put her face in it. She went down the row of them sniffing, bucket after bucket, her eyes half-shut and her nose buried in the petals, and as she went she talked, fast, mostly to herself. "Rhodinol. Lots of it. And geraniol, that's the sweet. Phenylethyl, that's the honey under it. This one's got eugenol, smell, clove, that's a damask, has to be. That's citronellol, lemony, see? This one's an old one, an old one, it's got a bit of musk." The growers stopped working and stared at her. One of them nudged another.

event: Elsie tells the growers Tilly is the cleverest person she knows, and Tilly goes pink to the ears.
prose: Elsie set down her bucket by the cart and went over to the growers. "She's an alchemist," she told them, proudly, as if she were showing them something she had made. "Tilly. She's the cleverest person I know. She can smell what anything's made of. She can make fire burn blue." The growers looked at Tilly again with different faces, and one of them nodded slowly, impressed. Tilly lifted her head out of a bucket of cream roses and heard. She stood with a rose petal stuck to the end of her nose, and went pink, and the pink went up and up until it reached the tips of her ears.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 22 → 23 (kindness: called the cleverest person Elsie knows)

event: On the road the reeds rustle, and a giggle comes out of them.
prose: They went on out of Sweetwater with the cart heavy now and smelling like a summer evening. The road bent close along the reed beds. The reeds stood higher than Tamsin's head here, thick and green and whispering, and as the cart came along beside them they began to rustle, though the air was still. Elsie looked. The rustling ran along the reeds beside the cart, keeping pace with it. And out of the green, from somewhere quite near, there came a giggle: a tiny, high, breathless giggle, like a girl's laugh heard through a keyhole, and then another, from a little further along.

event: A finger-long winged thing darts out and steals a rose off the cart.
prose: Something darted out of the reeds. It was so quick that Elsie saw it only as a flash: a thing the length of her finger, with wings like a dragonfly's buzzing to a blur, and a thin green body, and a face, a tiny pointed laughing face. It shot across the road in front of her nose and straight into the back of the cart, and came out again with a whole red rose in its arms, a rose bigger than itself, and zipped back into the reeds with it, the rose's stem trailing, and the reeds closed over it, and there came a whole chorus of giggling.

event: The carter says reed sprites: harmless, but they take anything bright.
prose: "Reed sprites," the carter said, sourly, without turning round. "There they are. Told you." She flicked the reins. "Harmless, mind. They don't bite and they don't sting. They just take. Anything bright. Flowers, ribbons, buttons, a shiny buckle, a hat with a feather in it. My good red hat went in there in the spring and I've not seen it since. They've a nest of stolen things somewhere in there the size of a haystack, I'll be bound." She jerked her chin at the rose stem lying in the road, dropped. "They'll strip the cart bare by Reedby if you let them. That's what you're for."

event: Tamsin swats at the next one and misses, and it giggles at her.
prose: Tamsin took it personally. She dropped back to walk at the tail of the cart, by the roses, with her fists up and her eyes on the reeds, and when the next sprite came darting out, a flash of green wings going for a white rose, she swung at it with her open hand, fast as anything. She missed. The sprite went over her hand and under her elbow and round her head once, close, so that her curls lifted in the wind of its wings, and then hung in the air just out of reach in front of her face and giggled at her, and stuck out a tiny tongue, and was gone.

event: Tilly flicks a drop of something sour at the reeds, and the sprites scatter sneezing.
prose: Tilly had been walking with her tongue between her teeth, sorting through the vials at her belt. Now she unstoppered a little brown one, sniffed it, made a face, and stoppered it again; then unstoppered a green one and nodded. She tipped a few drops of it into her palm and flicked them, wrist and fingers, out across the road at the reeds. A sharp sour smell went up, like vinegar and crushed ants, and Elsie's eyes watered. In the reeds there was a sudden storm of tiny sneezes, dozens of them, high and furious, and then a frantic whirring of wings going away fast in every direction.

event: At Larkford they load poppies, and Tilly falls asleep on the cart against Elsie's shoulder.
prose: Larkford was nearly all poppies. The fields came right down to the road on both sides, a red so bright and thick it seemed to hum, and the growers there had their buckets of them waiting, the flowers like crumpled silk. They loaded them in among the roses. Then there was a stretch of straight flat road in the sun, and the carter let them ride, and Elsie climbed up and sat on the back of the cart among the buckets with Tilly beside her. Tilly talked for a while about the sneezing mixture, and her words came slower and slower, and then her head dropped onto Elsie's shoulder, and she was asleep.

event: Elsie keeps very still so as to let her sleep, and tucks a poppy into her braid.
prose: Elsie kept very still. She sat with her back against a bucket and her legs hanging over the tail of the cart, swaying with it, and did not shift her shoulder, though it began after a while to ache, because Tilly's breathing had gone deep and slow against her neck, and her mouth had fallen a little open, and her goggles had slid crooked, and she looked very small and very tired. Elsie thought of her knocking twice at the Honeycomb last night with her fizz. Carefully, with her free hand, she took a poppy from the bucket beside her and tucked its stem into the top of Tilly's braid, where it sat like a flame.

event: Cora walks beside the cart watching the reeds, and her nose is going pink in the sun.
prose: Cora did not ride. She walked beside the cart on the reed side, as she had walked all morning, upright in her charcoal coat buttoned to the throat, with her hands clasped behind her back and her grey eyes moving steadily over the reeds, keeping watch for the next flash of wings. The sun was high and hot now. Elsie, swaying on the tail of the cart with Tilly asleep on her, watched her, and saw that the back of Cora's neck, between her collar and her tight black bun, had gone pink, and that the tip of her fine straight nose had gone pink too.

event: Elsie wets a broad dock leaf at a trough and lays it on the back of Cora's neck.
prose: At a crossroads beyond Larkford there was a stone horse trough with a pump. When the cart stopped to water the donkey Elsie eased Tilly's head down onto a folded sack, so gently that she slept on, and slid off the cart. A clump of dock grew by the trough. She picked the broadest leaf she could find, and dipped it in the cold water, and shook it, and went up behind Cora where she stood watching the reeds. "Hold still," Elsie said. And she laid the wet leaf, cool and dripping, flat across the back of Cora's sunburnt neck, above her collar, and smoothed it down with her palm.

event: Cora stands very still and leaves it there.
prose: Cora went still. She went entirely still, the way she had gone still over the tea cup on the guild stairs, her hands still clasped behind her back, her eyes still on the reeds. Water ran from the leaf down under her collar, and Elsie saw her shoulders tighten at the cold, and then slowly, slowly let go. She did not turn round. She did not reach up to take the leaf off. She stood there by the trough in the sun and let it stay, and after a moment Elsie saw her close her eyes, just for a breath, and open them again on the reeds.

changes.note: Bond: Cora 13 → 14 (kindness: a wet dock leaf for her sunburnt neck)

event: At Pennyfield the carters stop at the Poppy inn for the noon meal, and so do they.
prose: Pennyfield was the biggest of the villages, with a stone bridge over a brook and a squat church tower, and at the far end of its one street, under a painted sign of a red poppy, stood the Poppy inn. Carts were drawn up outside it in the shade of a chestnut tree, half a dozen of them, piled with hay and flour sacks and crates of hens, and their carters sat at long tables out on the cobbles with mugs in front of them. Their own carter pulled up among them and climbed down, stretching her back. "Noon," she said. "We eat." So they ate too.

event: They eat bread, cheese and cherries at an outside table, each paying for her own.
prose: They took an outside table under the chestnut, and a girl from the inn brought them each a plate: a heel of brown bread, a wedge of crumbly white cheese, and a heap of dark cherries still on their stalks. It was three pips a plate. Elsie counted three copper pips out of her purse into the girl's palm for her own, and Tamsin dug three out of her pocket, and Tilly, yawning, still with the poppy in her braid, found hers at the bottom of her apron among the corks. Cora had brought her own bread and cheese wrapped in a cloth, and unwrapped it neatly at the end of the bench.

event: Tilly asks, very casually, what Tamsin's bunk is like.
prose: Tilly ate her cherries very carefully, one at a time, laying each stone in a neat row on the edge of her plate. Halfway down the row she said, without looking up, in a voice so light and careless that it came out a little too high: "So what's it like? Tamsin's bunk?" She laid down another stone. "On a barge. I've not been on a barge. I just wondered what they're like. Bunks. On barges." She picked up another cherry and examined it closely. Cora, at the end of the bench, paused with her bread halfway to her mouth, and then went on eating.

event: Tamsin says narrow, and grins at Elsie, and Tilly stabs a cherry.
prose: "Narrow," Tamsin said. She leaned back on the bench with her long legs stretched out under the table and her hands behind her head, and grinned, crooked and slow, straight across the table at Elsie. "Very narrow." Elsie laughed. "It is," she said. "We were squashed flat. Tamsin nearly fell out, and I had to pull her back in." Tilly stabbed a cherry. She stabbed it with her fork, quite hard, right through, so that the juice spurted out red over her plate and onto her cuff, and then she looked at it in surprise as if someone else had done it, and ate it.

memory.fact: Elsie and Tamsin slept the night of the sixth together in Tamsin's bunk on the Marigold.

event: Elsie says she wishes they all lived under one roof, and the table goes quiet.
prose: Elsie looked round at them all: Tamsin stretched out in the sun, Tilly with cherry juice on her cuff and a poppy in her hair, Cora upright at the end of the bench with her lunch in its cloth and a damp patch on her collar where the leaf had been. A warm full feeling came up in her chest. "I wish we all lived under one roof," she said. "All of us. In one house, on a canal, with a kitchen, so we could have breakfast together every morning like on the barge." The table went quiet. Tamsin's grin stopped. Tilly stopped chewing. Cora set down her bread.

event: Cora says that is not how the guild works, and then writes in her ledger anyway.
prose: "That," Cora said, after a moment, "is not how the guild works." She said it in her flat exact voice, the voice for rules, looking at her bread. "A party is a party for the length of a notice. Then it's a name on a slate again." She brushed a crumb off the cloth. "It isn't a household." Then she opened her ledger on the table beside her plate, and uncapped her pen, and wrote a line, in her small hand, and Elsie watched her write it and could not see from across the table what it said.

event: Elsie asks what she's writing; Cora says skills used: none.
prose: "What are you writing?" Elsie asked. She asked it with real interest, leaning over the cherry stones. Cora finished the line. She capped the pen, and blotted the page with the corner of her cloth, and looked up at Elsie with her cool grey eyes, perfectly level. "Skills used," she said, "none." And she shut the ledger. Elsie laughed. Tamsin snorted into her mug. Tilly laughed a beat behind them, with her hand over her mouth full of cherry, and pointed at the ledger as if to say she remembered the cellar. Cora picked up her bread again, and the corner of her unsmiling mouth moved, very slightly, and was still.

event: Past Pennyfield the reeds grow thick right up to the road.
prose: Past Pennyfield the road went down into a long hollow where a slow stream fed the Mere, and the reeds grew thick there, thicker than anywhere yet, right up to the edge of the road on the left hand and in places across it, so that the cart's wheels crushed them. They stood far over Tamsin's head. The road was in green shade between them and the air was hot and still and smelled of mud. The carter sat up straight on her seat and gathered the reins short. "Here's the bad stretch," she said, low. "Here's where they live. Look sharp."

event: A cloud of sprites boils out of the reeds and mobs the cart, giggling.
prose: They came all at once. The reeds on the left hand heaved and rustled from end to end, and out of them boiled a cloud of sprites, dozens upon dozens, green wings buzzing like a swarm of bees, and the air was full of giggling, high and shrill and delighted, coming from everywhere. They mobbed the cart. They poured over the buckets and pulled at the roses and tugged at the poppies, two and three to a flower; they swarmed round the donkey's hat; they went for Tamsin's knuckle wraps and Tilly's brass goggles and the shiny buttons on Cora's coat. The carter swore and flapped her hat at them.

event: One snatches the pink-and-white clip from Elsie's hair and dives into the reeds.
prose: Elsie flapped too, laughing, with both hands, at the sprites going for the roses. Then she felt a tiny sharp tug at her scalp, just above her ear, and a whir of wings by her cheek. She put her hand up. Her clip was gone. She turned and saw it, already a yard away and rising: her pink-and-white clip, held in the arms of a single sprite and flashing in the sun as it went, and the sprite looking back at her over the top of it with its tiny face split by a grin. Then it dived. It dropped like a stone into the reeds, and they closed over it.

changes.note: A reed sprite snatches the flower clip from Elsie's hair
The sprite carries the clip off into the reeds
The clip is in the reed beds past Pennyfield, held by a sprite

event: Elsie's hand goes to her hair, and her eyes fill.
prose: Elsie's hand stayed in her hair where the clip had been. She felt the place, the little gap in the hair above her ear, with her fingertips, as if the clip might still be there and she had only missed it. It was not. Her eyes filled. They filled all at once and brimmed over and ran, and she stood in the road among the giggling and the buzzing with her hand pressed flat to the side of her head, and could not stop them. It was only a clip. She could not have said why it mattered so much, only that it did, and that the place above her ear felt cold and bare and wrong without it.

event: Tamsin is into the reeds up to her waist before anyone can stop her.
prose: Tamsin had seen. Elsie did not see her see it; she only heard a sound behind her, a kind of growl, and turned, and Tamsin was already gone off the road. She went into the reeds at a run, straight in where the sprite had gone, crashing through them with her arms up before her face, and the reeds swallowed her to the shoulders, and then she was in up to her waist in black water and mud and still going, shoving the reeds aside with both arms, shouting something at the sprites that Elsie could not catch, before anyone could so much as say her name.

event: Cora says reed beds swallow boots, and goes in after her, coat and all.
prose: "Reyes!" Cora said sharply. She took a step to the reed edge and looked down at the black mud where Tamsin had gone in, sucking and bubbling round the broken stems. "Reed beds swallow boots," she said to the reeds, quite calmly. "And then the legs in them." She looked down at her own black boots, and at the long skirts of her charcoal coat, buttoned to the throat. Then she stepped off the road into the reeds, coat and all, and the mud took her to the shin at once, and she waded after Tamsin with her ledger held high over her head in one hand.

event: Elsie and Tilly follow; the mud is warm and comes to their knees.
prose: Elsie wiped her face with the back of her wrist and went after them. Tilly, behind her, said, "Oh, oh no, oh, all right," and came too. The mud was warm. That was the surprising thing: it was warm as bathwater, thick and soft and black, and it came up over Elsie's boots and over her knees at the first step and held on, so that every step was a pull and a slow sucking let-go. The reeds closed over their heads, green and dim, and buzzed with sprites. Tilly held on to the back of Elsie's belt and waded, apologising to the mud.

event: They find the sprite on a reed head clutching the clip, with three others admiring it.
prose: They found it in a little clearing in the reeds where the water opened out, black and still, with the sky reflected in it. The sprite sat on the very top of a bending reed head, swaying, with Elsie's clip clutched to its chest in both arms. Three other sprites hovered round it in the air, close, admiring. One touched the pink enamel flower with a tiny finger. Another stroked the white. The first one turned the clip a little in the sun to show them how it shone, and they all made soft cooing sounds over it, like doves. Tamsin stood a few yards off, mud to the ribs, panting.

event: Elsie crouches in the mud and asks the sprite, politely, for her clip back.
prose: Elsie waded forward until she was close, and then crouched down in the mud, slowly, so as not to frighten it, until the warm black water was at her waist and her face was level with the reed head. The sprite watched her with bright black eyes like seeds. "Hello," Elsie said softly. "Excuse me. I'm so sorry to bother you. That's my clip, you see. It's very pretty, I know. I like it too." She held out her muddy hand, flat, palm up, under the reed. "Please may I have it back? I'd be ever so grateful. I'll find you something else bright."

event: The sprite giggles, shakes its head, and hugs the clip.
prose: The sprite giggled. It looked at her open hand, and at her wet face, and giggled, a tiny silvery sound, and shook its head hard from side to side so that its pointed ears flapped. Then it hugged the clip. It wrapped both arms and both legs tight round it, and pressed its cheek to the enamel flower, and shut its eyes in bliss, and rocked on the swaying reed head with it as if it were a baby. The three others giggled with it. One of them patted the clip, possessively. Elsie's face crumpled, and she let her hand fall into the mud.

event: Tilly takes two vials from her belt and mixes them into a small, steady blue flame.
prose: "Wait," Tilly said behind her. "Wait, wait, I've got— hang on." She let go of Elsie's belt and stood up straight in the mud, swaying, and pulled two vials from her belt, one clear and one a pale cloudy yellow. Her hands were shaking. She pulled the corks with her teeth and spat them into the reeds and tipped the yellow into the clear, a little, and a little more, and swirled it, frowning hard. Then it caught. A small steady blue flame stood up out of the neck of the vial, clean and bright and still, burning without a wick; and Tilly's hands went steady round it.

changes.note: Tilly gains 10 XP for Brew in the field: the blue flame (20 → 30)

memory.fact: Tilly can mix two vials into a small, steady blue flame that burns without a wick.
Tilly's shaking hands go steady the moment her brew catches.

event: The sprites go silent and stare at the blue flame, enchanted.
prose: The sprites went silent. All four of them, and all round the clearing in the reeds the giggling and buzzing stopped too, at once, as if a door had shut on it. The sprite on the reed head opened its eyes. It stared at the blue flame. They all stared, their tiny faces turned toward it and lit blue from underneath, their wings slowing and folding, their mouths open. Elsie saw it shine in every pair of seed-black eyes, a little blue spark, over and over, all round the clearing, dozens of them, rapt and still, as if they could not look at anything else.

event: Tilly sets the burning vial on a reed root, and the sprite drops the clip to go to it.
prose: Tilly waded a step closer, holding the flame up, slow. She bent and set the vial down on a thick knot of reed root that stood up out of the water, and settled it there carefully so it would not tip, and stepped back. The flame burned on, small and blue and steady, reflected in the black water underneath so that there seemed to be two. The sprite on the reed head looked at it. It looked down at the clip in its arms, pink and white. It looked at the flame. Then it let go of the clip entirely, and flew straight down to the blue flame.

event: Elsie snatches up the clip and kisses Tilly on the cheek, mud and all.
prose: The clip dropped. It fell turning through the air, flashing, and Elsie lunged and caught it an inch above the black water with both hands, and held it to her chest. She knelt there in the mud a moment with her eyes shut, holding it. Then she scrambled up, dripping to the waist, and turned round and threw her arms round Tilly's neck and kissed her on the cheek, hard and loud, smack, mud and all, so that a black smudge was left on Tilly's cheek in the shape of Elsie's mouth. "Tilly," she said. "Tilly, you're a wonder. You're a wonder."

changes.note: Elsie snatches the clip back when the sprite drops it
The clip is in Elsie's hand again

event: Tilly stands in the reeds with her hand on her cheek and forgets to walk.
prose: Tilly did not move. Elsie let go of her and turned away, laughing and wiping her eyes with the back of her wrist, but Tilly stayed exactly where she was, up to her knees in the warm mud among the reeds, with one hand lifted and pressed flat against her own cheek, over the place. Her blue eyes were enormous. Her mouth was a little open. She stood and stared at the reeds, holding her cheek, and when Elsie started back the way they had come and called her name, she did not follow. She seemed to have forgotten how, as if her legs belonged to somebody else.

event: Tamsin hauls her out by the collar, and Tilly is still holding her cheek.
prose: Tamsin came wading past her. She looked at Tilly, standing there like a post in the reeds with her hand on her cheek, and rolled her eyes, and reached out without stopping and took her by the back of her collar and towed her. Tilly came along behind her like a boat on a rope, stumbling and squelching through the mud, her boots coming out of it with loud sucking pops, her free arm flapping for balance. Her other hand stayed on her cheek the whole way back. Tamsin looked down at her once over her shoulder, and her mouth went crooked and odd, and she looked away.

event: Elsie pins the clip back in with muddy fingers, and Cora reaches over and straightens it.
prose: On the solid ground of the road Elsie stopped and pinned the clip back into her hair. Her fingers were black with mud and shaking a little, and she pushed it in above her ear, where it went, by feel, and it went in crooked and caught a lock of hair wrong. Cora came up out of the reeds behind her, mud to the knee, coat black to the hem, the ledger still held high and clean. She looked at Elsie's clip. Then she reached over, without a word, and took it between her finger and thumb, and slid it out, and set it in again, straight.

changes.note: Elsie pins the clip back in her hair; Cora straightens it

event: Cora's fingers stay a moment at Elsie's temple, and then she steps back.
prose: Cora's fingers did not leave at once. They stayed a moment at Elsie's temple, by the clip, very light, two fingertips resting against the side of her head just where the hair met the skin; and Elsie, standing still for her, could feel that they were cool, and that they were not quite steady. Cora was looking at the clip, not at Elsie's face, with her grey eyes very intent, as if she were checking her work. Then she seemed to notice where her hand was. She took it back, and stepped back with it, a full step, to her place behind Elsie, and clasped her hands behind her coat.

event: Back at the cart the carter laughs at the four of them, muddy to the thighs.
prose: The carter was sitting on the cart's seat where they had left her, with her hat back on and a heap of sprite-pulled petals in her lap, and the sprites gone quiet in the reeds behind her. She watched the four of them come squelching up out of the reed bed one after another onto the road: Tamsin black to the ribs, Tilly black to the thighs and holding her cheek, Elsie black to the waist with her clip on straight, and the Warden black to the knee with her ledger in her hand. And the carter put back her head and laughed and laughed until she had to hold on to the seat.

event: At Reedby they load the last buckets: lavender, cornflowers and sweet peas.
prose: Reedby, at the far end of the round, sat on a spit of land between the reeds and the open water, and grew a little of everything. The growers there had the last buckets waiting at the roadside: lavender in tight purple bundles, cornflowers bluer than the sky, and sweet peas in every soft colour, pink and mauve and white and the dark red of wine, smelling so sweet that Elsie put her face in a bucket of them the way Tilly had done at Sweetwater and breathed. They loaded them on top of everything else, wherever they would fit, until the cart was heaped up high.

pictured.coverAfter: Reedby, at the far end of the round, sat on a spit

event: The growers let them wash at the horse trough, and Tamsin dunks her whole head.
prose: The growers looked at the mud on them and laughed, but kindly, and took them round to the horse trough in the yard behind the last cottage, and let them wash. Elsie scrubbed her arms and her knees and as much of her legs as she could reach, and the water went black. Tilly, still pink, scrubbed her cheek very lightly round the mud smudge without quite washing it off. Cora washed her boots, and wrung out the hem of her coat. And Tamsin took one look at the trough, and bent over it, and plunged her whole head in, curls and all, right up to the shoulders.

event: Tamsin shakes her curls like a dog over Tilly, and Tilly shrieks and laughs.
prose: She came up streaming, gasping, laughing, with her copper curls flattened dark to her head and water pouring off her chin and down her front. Tilly was standing right beside her, wringing out a cuff. Tamsin looked at her sideways, and grinned, and shook her head like a dog, hard, so that her curls whipped round and flung water out in a great glittering spray all over Tilly. Tilly shrieked. She leapt back, dripping, with her hands up and her goggles fogged, and then she was laughing, laughing so hard she had to sit down on the edge of the trough, and Tamsin laughed too, and splashed her again.

event: On the road home the cart is so full of flowers the donkey walks in a cloud of scent.
prose: They turned the cart for home in the late afternoon. It was so heaped with flowers now that the buckets stood two deep and the donkey had to lean into the collar on every rise, and the scent came off the load in waves, roses and lavender and sweet peas, so thick and sweet that the donkey walked along the shore road in a cloud of it, with bees following. Elsie's legs were stiff with drying mud. Her halter was damp. Her clip was in her hair. The sun stood well over to the west above the Mere, and the water glittered, and she was very happy.

event: Elsie asks Cora what she likes besides tea; Cora thinks a long while and says quiet.
prose: Cora walked beside her. Elsie had been thinking for some time, since the trough, and now she said, "Cora? What do you like? Besides tea." Cora looked at her. "Like," she said. "Yes. Things you like. Black tea, strong, one sugar, I know that one. What else?" Cora turned her face back to the road. She walked for a long while without answering, past the end of one lavender field and the start of another, so long that Elsie thought she had decided not to. Then she said, very low, as if she were telling her something she had only just found out herself: "Quiet."

memory.fact: Besides strong black tea, Cora likes quiet.
Besides strong black tea, Cora likes quiet.

event: Elsie walks beside her in quiet for a whole field after that, and Cora looks at her twice.
prose: Elsie nodded. She did not ask anything more. She walked on beside Cora in the afternoon sun and kept her mouth closed, not humming, not talking, all the way along the next field, a long one, poppies, with the cart squeaking ahead of them and the bees going by and Tamsin and Tilly's voices far up at the front, and she let the quiet be Cora's. It was harder than she had expected. Halfway along the field Cora looked at her, a short sideways look, and away. Near the end of it she looked again, and that time her look stayed a moment longer before it went back to the road.

event: Tilly rides on the cart's tail among the buckets, swinging her muddy boots.
prose: Tilly had climbed up onto the tail of the cart, where Elsie had sat in the morning, and was riding there among the buckets of sweet peas with her back against them and her legs hanging down over the edge. Her boots were caked grey with dried mud to the ankle, and she swung them, one and then the other, kicking at the dust of the road as it went by beneath her. The poppy had gone limp in her braid. She was humming something tuneless. She still had the faint grey smudge on her cheek, and as Elsie came up alongside she saw Tilly touch it.

event: Elsie climbs up beside her; Tilly touches her cheek and asks if Elsie kisses everyone.
prose: Elsie hopped up onto the tail of the cart beside her, and the cart dipped and swayed, and Tilly grabbed a bucket and laughed. They sat side by side swinging their legs. After a while Tilly touched the smudge on her cheek with two fingers, looking down at her boots. "Elsie," she said. "Back there. In the reeds." She rubbed the smudge with her thumb. "Do you kiss everyone? Like that? When they get your things back? Is it a thing you do?" She laughed, a small embarrassed laugh, and swung her boots harder. "I only wondered. I didn't know where to put my feet, after."

event: Elsie says only people she loves, and kisses the other cheek to make it fair.
prose: "Oh, Tilly," Elsie said. She thought about it for a moment, swinging her legs. Then she said, quite seriously, "Only people I love." She looked at Tilly's cheek, the grey smudge on the one side and the clean freckled other. "And I only did the one side, didn't I? That's not fair on the other." And before Tilly could say anything she leaned over and kissed her on the clean cheek, soft and quick, with a little smack, and sat back. "There," she said. "Now they match." She smiled at Tilly, pleased with herself, and swung her legs.

event: Tilly goes so red the carter asks if she's had too much sun.
prose: Tilly went red. She went red the way a kettle comes to the boil, slowly and then all at once, from her collar up her throat and over both cheeks and the smudge and her ears and right up into her hairline under the goggles, until she was as red as the limp poppy in her braid, redder, and she put both hands over her face. The carter glanced back over her shoulder from the seat and frowned at her. "You all right back there, girl?" she said. "You've gone scarlet. Had too much sun, I shouldn't wonder. Get your hat on." Tilly made a muffled noise into her hands.

event: They come into the city as the lamplighters' boats set out along the canals.
prose: They came into the city at dusk. The lake had gone violet behind them, and as the cart rolled in over the first bridge the lamplighters' boats were setting out along the canals, low narrow boats with a man or a woman standing in the stern of each with a long pole and a flame at the end of it, poling from lantern to lantern. One by one the paper lanterns along the towpaths caught and glowed, red and gold and white, and their light ran out across the dark water and shook there. The donkey's ears pricked. He knew where he was. He picked up his feet for home.

memory.fact: Paper lanterns hang along every canal, and lamplighters' boats light them at dusk.

event: At the flower market the carter unloads into the stalls and pays them the notice.
prose: At the old flower market the stall-keepers were waiting with their lamps lit. The carter drew up, and they all set to unloading, handing the buckets down from the cart into the stalls, roses and poppies and lavender and sweet peas, until the market was a field of flowers under the lanterns and the cart stood light and empty. Then the carter climbed down and stood in front of the three of them, Elsie and Tamsin and Tilly, and dug in her smock, and counted out five silver lanterns, one at a time, into Elsie's cupped hands. "There," she said. "Worth every pip. Good round, that. Fewest roses lost since spring."

event: Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly share it out, and Elsie puts the odd pips in Tilly's hand.
prose: They shared it out on the edge of a stall under a lantern. Elsie gave Tamsin one silver lantern and Tilly one, and kept one, and took the other two to the flower-seller at the next stall, who changed them for twenty copper pips out of her apron. Elsie counted six pips into Tamsin's palm, and six into her own, and six into Tilly's. Two copper pips were left in her hand. She looked at them, and at Tilly, and folded Tilly's fingers over them. "Those are yours," she said. "For the blue flame." Tilly looked down at the two pips in her fist, and then at Elsie, and swallowed.

event: Cora walks them to the guild hall door as it shuts, writes the notice in, and goes off duty.
prose: Cora walked them back to the guild hall, through the lamplit squares, with her coat stiff with dried mud to the knee. The clerk was just shutting the great doors as they came up. Cora stopped him with a hand, and went in, and Elsie through the gap saw her at the desk under the last lamp opening the ledger and writing the notice in, the date and the pay and the names, in her small exact hand, and blotting it, and shutting it. Then she came out again, and stood on the step, and the doors closed behind her with a boom. "I'm off duty," Cora said. "Goodnight, Fairweather."

memory.fact: Cora goes off duty at the guild hall door when the hall shuts for the day.

event: Elsie gives her a lavender sprig saved from the last bucket; Cora tucks it in her buttonhole.
prose: "Wait," Elsie said. "Wait, Cora, I saved you something." She felt in her satchel, and brought out a sprig of lavender, a long one, that she had taken from the very last bucket at Reedby and kept safe all the way home between the pages of her notebook, so that it had come out flat and only a little crushed and still smelling sweet. She held it out on her palm. Cora looked at it. Then she took it, carefully, by the stem, and turned it once in her fingers, and slid it into the buttonhole of her charcoal coat, at the throat. She inclined her head. Then she turned and walked away across the square.

changes.note: Bond: Cora 14 → 15 (kindness: a lavender sprig, taken)

event: Tamsin says she's due on the Marigold for supper, and asks if Elsie will come.
prose: Elsie watched the lavender go off across the square on the dark coat, a small spot of colour, until Cora turned the corner. Beside her Tamsin cleared her throat. "I'm due on the Marigold," she said. "For supper. I promised." She shifted from foot to foot and rubbed the back of her neck. "You heard me promise. Twice." She looked at Elsie sideways, with her wet-dried curls springing everywhere. "Come with me? Mum'd be glad. Nell would. There'll be stew again, probably. Mum does stew when she's glad." She grinned, but it was a hopeful grin, not a sure one. "Will you come?"

event: Elsie says tonight Nell should have Tamsin to herself, and Tamsin should go.
prose: Elsie wanted to. She wanted to so much that she felt it in her chest: the low cabin, the stove, Rosa's laugh, the squeezebox, Tamsin's narrow bunk. Then she thought of Nell up on the cabin roof among the geraniums, with her scarred hand, saying I write her every week. She shook her head. "Not tonight," she said. "Tonight's Nell's. She's waited a year. You should go on your own, and sit with her, and let her have you all to herself, every bit." She took Tamsin's hand and squeezed it. "Go on. And tell your mum I'll save her a big slice."

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 34 → 36 (stand: Elsie gives up supper so Nell has her)

event: Tamsin hugs her hard, and runs for the Long Cut.
prose: Tamsin looked at her. Something came down the Tether, warm and sudden and so strong that Elsie caught her breath. Then Tamsin stepped forward and hugged her, hard, both arms right round her and her face pressed into Elsie's hair beside the clip, so hard that Elsie's feet came off the step. She held on a long moment. She did not say anything. Then she let go, and stepped back, and turned, and ran: off across the square in the lantern light toward the Long Cut, her boots loud on the stones, her curls bouncing, her axe on her back, and she did not look back once.

event: Tilly walks Elsie to Thimble Canal, swinging their joined hands.
prose: Tilly walked Elsie home. They went along Thimble Canal under the lanterns, and somewhere along the way, Elsie could not have said when, their hands had found each other, and Tilly swung them, their joined hands, forward and back between them as they walked, high, like children, and Elsie laughed and let her. Tilly talked. She talked about the sneezing mixture and the blue flame and the sprites' faces and what a sprite might be made of, very fast, in a happy tumble, and every time she ran out of breath she swung their hands higher, and Elsie swung them back.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 24 → 25 (kindness: hands joined along Thimble Canal)

event: At the Honeycomb door Tilly says goodnight, then says it again, and goes.
prose: At the Honeycomb's door, under its painted sign, Tilly stopped, and let go of Elsie's hand, and stood on the step. "Goodnight," she said. "Goodnight, Elsie." She went down one step backwards, and stopped, and looked up at Elsie under the lamp, with her goggles crooked and the limp poppy still in her braid and her cheek still faintly grey. "Goodnight," she said again, and laughed at herself, and went pink. Then she turned and went off along the canal at a half run, her braids bouncing, and Elsie stood in the doorway and watched her until she had gone round the bend.

event: In the attic Elsie scrubs the reed mud off her legs at the basin.
prose: Up in the attic Elsie lit the candle and pulled off her boots, which were stiff as wood with dried mud, and stood them by the door. Then she poured the chipped jug into the basin and sat on the stool with one foot in it at a time, and scrubbed. The reed mud had dried on her legs in a grey crust from her knees down, cracked like an old plate, and under it her skin was pink and tender from the sun. She scrubbed with the cloth until the water in the basin was black, and threw it out of the round window into the canal, and filled it again, and scrubbed some more.

event: She waters the plants and tells Captain the mint about the sprites.
prose: When she was clean and in her shift, she went to the crate under the round window and watered the plants, one at a time, as she did every night: Mrs Pennywhistle the fern first, then Sunny, then Doris, who wanted very little, then Captain. She crouched by the mint with the jug. "There are sprites in the reeds by the lake," she told him in a low voice, "about as long as your tallest leaf, with wings like dragonflies, and they steal anything bright. One stole my clip. Tilly got it back with a blue flame." She thought. "You'd have liked them. They giggle." Captain smelled of mint.

memory.fact: Elsie's plants live in their crate under the attic's round window.

event: She writes in her notebook: Tilly, blue flame, cheek; Cora, quiet.
prose: She sat down at the rocking little table, and got out her notebook, and opened it at the page of names. The lavender sprig had left a faint purple print on the paper where it had lain all the way home. She dipped her pen. Under Tilly, she wrote: blue flame, and then, after a moment, cheek. She looked at that, and smiled, and left it. Then she went down the page to Cora, where it said black, strong, one sugar, and under that, in her round careful hand, she wrote: quiet. She sat and looked at the word for a while, and blew on the ink.

memory.fact: Elsie keeps a notebook of the birthdays and favourite things of people she loves.

event: Through the Tether she feels Tamsin across the city, loud and warm and laughing.
prose: She blew out the candle and lay down on the narrow bed. Through the round window the canal lanterns made gold shapes on the sloped ceiling, and they shook when a boat went by. Elsie lay on her back with her hands folded on her stomach and felt for the thread. It was there, as it was each night now, running out from under her breastbone across the dark city to the Long Cut; and from the far end of it, faint with distance but plain, came Tamsin: loud, and warm, and laughing, laughing so hard Elsie could feel it shake. Elsie laughed too, out loud, alone in the attic, without knowing why.

event: The baker climbs the narrow stairs with a slice of honey cake on a plate, sets it down, and goes.
prose: There were footsteps on the narrow stairs: slow, heavy, careful ones, coming up from the bakery. Elsie sat up. There was a knock, one, and the door opened, and Agnes came in with a candle in one hand and a plate in the other, and on the plate, on a square of brown paper, a thick slice of honey cake, golden, with the dip in the middle. Agnes set it down on the little table beside the notebook. She looked at the muddy boots by the door, and at Elsie sitting up in bed, and nodded once. Then she went out, and the door closed, and her footsteps went slowly down.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 36 → 37 (Tether: under it by her own wish at day's end)
